The song is 'new' because it celebrates the new exodus and new creation accomplished by the Lamb's death. In 14:3 only the redeemed can learn it.
By Your blood You purchased for God those from every tribe and tongue and people and nation

God redeemed Israel from slavery in Egypt to be his own possession (Exodus 15:13, 16; Deuteronomy 7:8). The fourfold formula echoes Daniel's 'peoples, nations and languages' who serve the son of man (Daniel 3:4; 7:14) and the table of nations in Genesis 10. The promise that all families of the earth would be blessed in Abraham stands behind it (Genesis 12:3).

Agorazō is market language, used of buying slaves; Ephesus and other Asian cities had large slave markets, and manumission by payment was common. Roman propaganda celebrated the empire's rule over many peoples, as in the Sebasteion at Aphrodisias with its reliefs of conquered nations.

The Lamb's death is a ransom that transfers people from bondage into God's ownership, forming a multinational people. The fourfold formula (used seven times in Revelation in varying order) signals universality and counters Rome's claim to rule the nations.
You have made them to be a kingdom and priests to serve our God

At Sinai Israel is called to be 'a kingdom of priests and a holy nation' (Exodus 19:6); Isaiah promises that God's people will be called priests of the LORD (Isaiah 61:6). Jubilees 16:18 and 33:20 echo the Exodus 19 vocation.
Priesthoods of the imperial cult were prestigious civic honours held by the elite of Asia's cities; John gives the status of priest to ordinary, often marginal, believers.

The Sinai vocation of Israel is now given to the Lamb's multinational people, who mediate God's presence and serve him as priest-kings (covenantal interpreters speak of fulfilment; dispensationalists hold that Israel's own national calling still awaits fulfilment). Revelation 1:6 states this as already true.
They will reign upon the earth

Daniel promises that the kingdom and dominion under the whole heaven will be given to 'the people of the saints of the Most High' (Daniel 7:18, 22, 27). Psalm 37:11 promises the meek will inherit the land.

The redeemed share Christ's rule on earth. There is a textual variant: some manuscripts read the future 'they will reign' (basileusousin), others the present 'they reign' (basileuousin); most modern editions prefer the future, but the reading and its timing are debated, which makes this verse a minor text in the millennial discussion.

Historic premillennialists (Ladd) see the future tense as pointing to the saints' reign with Christ on the earth during the millennium after his return (Revelation 20:4-6), continuing into the new creation.
Dispensational premillennialists (Walvoord) read it as the church reigning with Christ over the earth in the future thousand-year kingdom, in which promises to national Israel are also fulfilled.

Amillennialists (Beale, Hoekema) note the present-tense variant and Revelation 1:6, and see believers reigning now in a real but hidden way with Christ (spiritually, through faithful witness and with the souls of the departed in heaven), consummated in the new heaven and new earth of chapters 21-22.
Postmillennialists (Gentry, Chilton) see the saints' reign as begun already and expanding in history as the gospel progressively subdues the nations (Daniel 2:35, 44; 7:27), before Christ returns.
Myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands

Before the Ancient of Days stand 'a thousand thousands ... ten thousand times ten thousand' (Daniel 7:10). The LORD comes from Sinai with myriads of holy ones (Deuteronomy 33:2; Psalm 68:17). 1 Enoch 14:22 and 40:1 describe innumerable angels around the throne.
An uncountable angelic host joins the worship. The language is deliberately beyond calculation, stressing the immensity of heaven's acclamation.
'Worthy is the Lamb ... to receive power and riches and wisdom and strength and honor and glory and blessing'
David's prayer ascribes greatness, power, glory, victory, majesty, riches and honour to God (1 Chronicles 29:10-13), the closest Old Testament parallel to this sevenfold doxology.
Imperial acclamations and honorific inscriptions ascribed power, wealth and glory to the emperor; such lists of virtues and honours were standard in civic praise.
Seven attributes signal complete praise. The Lamb receives the honours that 1 Chronicles reserves for God, a clear claim of the Lamb's divine worthiness.
Every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea: 'To Him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb'
Psalm 148 summons every part of creation to praise the LORD, and Psalm 150:6 calls everything that has breath. The people answer doxologies with 'Amen' (1 Chronicles 16:36; Nehemiah 8:6).

Worship expands in widening circles until all creation acknowledges God and the Lamb together. Bauckham argues this joint worship includes Jesus in the identity of the one God without abandoning Jewish monotheism, since elsewhere John forbids worshipping angels (19:10; 22:8-9). The creatures' 'Amen' seals the liturgy.

Partial preterists see Christ's ascension and coronation (Daniel 7:13-14) in the taking of the scroll, and the scroll itself as the covenant judgment document against first-century Israel, opened in the events leading to AD 70 (Chilton, Gentry). The Lamb's worthiness rests on his finished work, and his kingdom of priests is the new-covenant people replacing the old priestly order.

Historicists (Elliott, Barnes) read chapter 5 as Christ's investiture with authority to reveal and direct the course of history; the seven-sealed scroll is the book of future events from the late first century onward, unfolded in sequence.

Dispensational futurists (Walvoord, Thomas) interpret the scroll as the title deed to the earth and the scene as a future heavenly event preceding the tribulation, in which Christ, as kinsman-redeemer, begins to reclaim the world through the seal judgments; the promised reign 'upon the earth' points to the coming millennial kingdom.

Idealists (Hendriksen, Poythress) see the Lamb's enthronement at the ascension and the scroll as God's plan for all history, which the crucified and risen Christ now administers; the chapter assures every generation of believers that history is in the hands of the slain Lamb.

Beale and Bauckham present chapter 5 as the inaugurated fulfilment of Daniel 7: Christ's death and resurrection have begun the latter-day kingdom, which will be consummated at his return. Bauckham stresses the reinterpretation of messianic war (Lion to Lamb) and the inclusion of the Lamb in divine worship.
Why does John hear about a Lion but see a Lamb? How does this reshape expectations of how God conquers evil?
Which interpretation of the scroll (title deed, covenant lawsuit, will, or plan of history) best fits Ezekiel 2, Daniel 12 and the rest of Revelation?
What does it mean that the Lamb stands 'in the center of the throne' and is worshipped alongside God?
How might believers facing pressure to offer incense to the emperor have heard 5:8?
Does 'they will reign upon the earth' (5:10) describe a present reality, a future millennium or the new creation?
The Six Seals and the Four Horsemen

The Lamb breaks the first six seals. At each of the first four, a living creature calls 'Come!' and a horseman rides out: a white horse whose crowned archer goes out conquering, a red horse whose rider removes peace with a great sword, a black horse whose rider holds scales amid famine prices, and a pale horse ridden by Death with Hades following, given power over a quarter of the earth. The fifth seal shows the souls of martyrs under the altar crying 'How long?' and being told to rest until their number is complete. The sixth seal brings a great earthquake and cosmic collapse, and people of every rank hide in caves from the wrath of God and the Lamb, asking who can stand.
First seal: the white horse
Second seal: the red horse
Third seal: the black horse and famine prices
Fourth seal: the pale horse, Death and Hades
Fifth seal: the souls under the altar
Sixth seal: cosmic upheaval and the great day of wrath

The horsemen are adapted from Zechariah, whose coloured horses patrol the earth (Zechariah 1:8-11) and whose four chariots with red, black, white and dappled horses go out to the four winds of heaven (Zechariah 6:1-8). Their effects (sword, famine, pestilence and wild beasts) are the classic covenant curses of Leviticus 26:21-26 and Ezekiel 14:21, and the sequence of war, famine, plague and persecution followed by cosmic signs closely parallels Jesus' Olivet Discourse (Matthew 24:6-29; Mark 13; Luke 21:9-26). The fifth seal draws on the theology of blood at the altar (Leviticus 4:7; 17:11) and on Jewish texts in which the righteous dead ask how long until judgment and are told to wait until a fixed number is complete (1 Enoch 47:1-4; 4 Ezra 4:35-37). The sixth seal reuses the prophets' language of de-creation for the fall of nations (Isaiah 13:10; 34:4; Joel 2:10, 31; Hosea 10:8; Isaiah 2:19-21).

For first-century Asia the imagery was vivid: the Parthian mounted archers beyond the Euphrates were Rome's most feared enemy and had defeated Roman armies (Crassus at Carrhae in 53 BC; a Roman army at Rhandeia in AD 62); civil war shook the empire in the 'year of four emperors' (AD 68-69); grain shortages and price spikes were frequent, and Domitian's edict of AD 92 restricting new vineyards in the provinces (Suetonius, Domitian 7) was resisted in Asia and withdrawn; and earthquakes devastated Asian cities (Sardis and others in AD 17, Laodicea c. AD 60). How these images relate to history is exactly where the interpretive schools part ways, and whether the seals are sequential, overlapping or recapitulated by the trumpets and bowls is itself disputed.
The Lamb opened one of the seals, and a living creature said, 'Come!'

In Ezekiel 10:6-7 a cherub hands out fire for judgment on Jerusalem; in Zechariah 6:5-8 the horses go out at God's command. Woes and judgments issuing from the heavenly sanctuary are typical of the prophets.

Every disaster that follows is unleashed only when the Lamb opens a seal and a throne-creature commands it; the passive 'was given' recurs through the chapter. Evil and suffering are thus placed under the sovereign permission of God and the Lamb. Some later manuscripts add 'and see' (hence the KJV), but the shorter text 'Come!' is best attested; most take it as a summons to the riders, not to John.
A white horse; its rider held a bow, was given a crown, and rode out to overcome and conquer

Zechariah's horses include white ones (Zechariah 1:8; 6:3, 6). The bow is God's weapon of judgment (Habakkuk 3:9; Psalm 7:12-13) and the weapon of invading nations (Jeremiah 50:42). Ezekiel 39:3 pictures God striking the bow from the hand of Gog.

The mounted archer was the signature of the Parthians, Rome's great rival in the east, who rode white horses in some depictions and humiliated Roman armies (Carrhae, 53 BC; Rhandeia, AD 62). White horses also drew the chariot of a Roman general in a triumph.

The identity of the first rider is one of Revelation's most debated questions. The parallels with the other three riders (all destructive, all 'given' authority) suggest conquest or militarism; the white colour and victory language suggest to others Christ or the gospel (compare 19:11). Many modern scholars see either military conquest or a satanic counterfeit of Christ.

Hendriksen, following Irenaeus and many Reformed interpreters, identifies the rider as Christ (or the gospel) going forth in victory throughout the church age, compared with Revelation 19:11 and Psalm 45:4-5; the other horsemen then picture the persecution and suffering that accompany the gospel's advance.

Chilton reads the rider as Christ going forth in judgment against Israel (the Roman armies serving as his instrument), while other preterists see the Roman advance under Vespasian and Titus against Judea in AD 66-70.

Walvoord, Thomas and most dispensationalists identify the rider as the future Antichrist, a false messiah who imitates Christ and initially conquers by diplomacy (a bow without arrows) at the start of the tribulation, in line with Matthew 24:5.

Elliott and Barnes read the white horse as the prosperous, victorious era of the Roman empire from Nerva through the Antonines (AD 96-180), with Elliott linking the bow to the Cretan origin of Nerva's line; others in the tradition saw the early triumph of Christianity.

Beale and many recent scholars see a satanic counterfeit or the forces of conquest and deception that oppress believers throughout the age, while acknowledging Parthian overtones for John's first readers.
A bright red horse; its rider took peace from the earth and was given a great sword

Zechariah's first rider sits on a red horse (Zechariah 1:8). The sword is the first of the covenant curses (Leviticus 26:25; Ezekiel 14:17), and God sometimes sets enemies against one another (Judges 7:22; Ezekiel 38:21; Zechariah 14:13).

The Pax Romana was celebrated as Augustus' gift to the world (the Ara Pacis in Rome; 'peace' on coins). Removing peace attacks Rome's core boast. The civil wars of AD 68-69 and the Jewish revolt (66-70) showed how fragile it was.
The red horse brings bloodshed, war and civil strife, 'men slaying one another'. Some see in 'slay' (sphazō, the verb used of the Lamb) a hint that believers too are slain in this violence.
Preterists point to the factional slaughter in Judea and Jerusalem during the Jewish War, vividly described by Josephus, and to the empire-wide turmoil of 68-69.
Elliott and Barnes saw the bloody civil wars and military anarchy after Commodus (from c. AD 185), when emperors were repeatedly murdered by their own soldiers.
Futurists see a future global war in the first half of the tribulation, removing the false peace brought by the first rider.
Idealists see war and civil strife as a recurring feature of every era between Christ's comings, as Jesus said (Matthew 24:6-7).
A black horse; its rider held a pair of scales

Zechariah 6:2 has black horses. Eating bread 'by weight' is a sign of famine under covenant judgment (Leviticus 26:26; Ezekiel 4:10, 16), and black is associated with famine-darkened faces (Lamentations 4:8; 5:10).
Scales (zygos) were the instrument of market officials and grain dealers; famine meant rationed food weighed out at high prices.
The black horse represents scarcity and economic hardship, often the aftermath of war. The scales show food being measured out sparingly.
A quart of wheat for a denarius, three quarts of barley for a denarius; do not harm the oil and wine

Oil, wine and grain are the staples of the covenant blessings and their withdrawal (Deuteronomy 7:13; 28:51; Joel 1:10; Hosea 2:8-9). Josephus describes the extreme famine and food prices during the siege of Jerusalem (Jewish War 5-6).

A denarius was roughly a labourer's daily wage (Matthew 20:2), and a choinix (about a quart) of wheat was one person's daily ration, so prices are roughly eight to sixteen times normal: a day's work feeds only the worker, or with cheaper barley a small family. Domitian's edict of AD 92 ordering vineyards in the provinces to be cut back to boost grain was resisted in Asia and withdrawn (Suetonius, Domitian 7), which some link to the protection of oil and wine; Asia was a major wine and olive region.

The voice from among the living creatures limits the famine: basic grain is ruinously expensive while oil and wine, longer-rooted crops, are spared. The judgment is real but restrained, a warning rather than total destruction. Whether 'oil and wine' points to luxury goods untouched for the rich, or to a merciful limit, is debated.
Preterists cite Josephus' accounts of soaring grain prices in besieged Jerusalem and the earlier famine under Claudius (Acts 11:28).

Elliott and Barnes applied it to the oppressive fiscal policy and grain taxation of the Roman empire in the early third century (from Caracalla onward), with scales signifying the administration of justice and revenue.
Futurists see a literal worldwide famine in the coming tribulation in which daily wages buy only a day's food.
Idealists read it as economic hardship and scarcity recurring throughout history, often falling hardest on the poor and on believers excluded from trade (compare 13:17).
A pale green horse; its rider's name was Death, and Hades followed

Death and Sheol (Hades in Greek) are paired and personified in Hosea 13:14, Isaiah 28:15-18 and Psalm 49:14. Zechariah 6:3 has dappled horses. Pestilence (thanatos in the Greek Old Testament often renders 'plague') is a covenant curse (Leviticus 26:25; Jeremiah 14:12).
Chlōros means yellowish-green, the colour of fresh vegetation but also of a corpse or of a person stricken by fear or sickness. Greek myth personified Thanatos (Death) and Hades the underworld god.

The fourth rider sums up the preceding horrors and adds plague: Death takes the body and Hades the soul. Christ holds the keys of Death and Hades (1:18), and in the end both are thrown into the lake of fire (20:14).
Authority over a fourth of the earth, to kill by sword, famine, plague and the beasts of the earth

God's 'four dreadful judgments' on Jerusalem are sword, famine, wild beasts and plague (Ezekiel 14:21; compare Ezekiel 5:12, 17; Jeremiah 15:2-3; Leviticus 26:22-26). Wild beasts as a curse appear in Leviticus 26:22 and Deuteronomy 32:24.
The fourfold list echoes covenant curse language, and the 'fourth' limits the scope, showing restraint; the trumpets raise it to a third (8:7-12) and the bowls are unlimited, suggesting escalation.

Because Ezekiel 14:21 is aimed specifically at Jerusalem, preterists (Chilton, Gentry) see the seals as the covenant curses of Leviticus 26 falling on the land of Israel ('the earth' as 'the land') in the Jewish War.
Futurists take a quarter of the world's population as a literal death toll in the future tribulation.
Idealists see partial, warning judgments on a rebellious world throughout history, short of final judgment.
Under the altar, the souls of those slain for the word of God and their testimony

The blood of sacrifices was poured out at the base of the altar (Leviticus 4:7; Exodus 29:12), and 'the life of the flesh is in the blood' (Leviticus 17:11), so the martyrs' lives are pictured as sacrifices poured out. Later rabbinic tradition placed the souls of the righteous beneath God's throne (Babylonian Talmud Shabbat 152b; later than Revelation). Paul describes his coming death as a drink offering (2 Timothy 4:6; Philippians 2:17).
Christians in Asia had already died for their witness, such as Antipas at Pergamum (Revelation 2:13); Nero's persecution in Rome (AD 64) was the most notorious early case.

The martyrs' deaths are counted as sacrifices offered to God, and they are kept safe in his presence. The altar here (whether altar of sacrifice or of incense, debated) connects their deaths with the prayers of 5:8 and 8:3-5.

Preterists link these martyrs to Jesus' warning that all the righteous blood shed on earth would come upon his generation and Jerusalem (Matthew 23:34-36; Luke 11:50-51), the city that killed the prophets; vengeance comes in AD 70.
Elliott and Barnes applied the fifth seal to the great Diocletianic persecution (AD 303-311), the climax of pagan Rome's war on the church.
Futurists generally identify them as believers martyred in the future tribulation (some include earlier martyrs), awaiting resurrection at Christ's return.
Idealists see the martyrs of every age, whose blood cries to God, and the intermediate state of the faithful dead, conscious and at rest with God.
'How long, O Lord, holy and true, until You avenge our blood?'

'How long?' is the cry of the lament psalms and prophets (Psalm 13:1-2; 79:5-10; 94:3; Habakkuk 1:2; Zechariah 1:12). Psalm 79:10 asks God to avenge the shed blood of his servants; Deuteronomy 32:43 promises he will. Abel's blood cries from the ground (Genesis 4:10). In 1 Enoch 47:1-4 the blood and prayers of the righteous rise to God demanding judgment, and in 4 Ezra 4:35-37 the souls of the righteous in their chambers ask 'how long', and are told to wait until the number is fulfilled.
Roman courts had condemned believers; the martyrs appeal from those courts to the true Judge, 'holy and true'.
The cry is not personal revenge but an appeal for God's justice and the public vindication of his name and people. The rest of the book, especially 16:5-7 and 19:2, answers it.
Each was given a white robe and told to rest a little while longer
White garments signify purity and heavenly vindication (Daniel 11:35; 12:10; 1 Enoch 62:15-16). Rest for the righteous dead appears in Isaiah 57:2 and Daniel 12:13.
The martyrs receive God's verdict of vindication now, even though public judgment on their persecutors is delayed. The robe anticipates 7:9-14 and the promise to overcomers (3:5).
Until the full number of their fellow servants, their brothers, were killed

The idea that the end awaits a fixed number of the righteous is found in 1 Enoch 47:4 ('the number of the righteous has been reached') and in 4 Ezra 4:36-37, where the archangel Jeremiel says the end will come when the number like the speaker is complete; 2 Baruch 23:4-5 has a similar thought.
God's apparent delay is purposeful: history continues until the full company of faithful witnesses has completed its testimony. It warns that more martyrdom lies ahead (fulfilled in 11:7 and 13:7).
There was a great earthquake
The earth quakes at God's coming in judgment (Isaiah 13:13; 24:18-20; Joel 2:10; Haggai 2:6-7; Ezekiel 38:19-20). Earthquakes also attended Sinai (Exodus 19:18).

Asia Minor was earthquake-prone: a great quake in AD 17 destroyed Sardis, Philadelphia and other cities (Tacitus, Annals 2.47), and Laodicea was devastated c. AD 60. Readers would know the terror firsthand.
The earthquake opens the sixth seal's scene of cosmic shaking, the prophetic language for God's intervention to overthrow powers. Earthquakes punctuate the book's climaxes (8:5; 11:13, 19; 16:18).
The sun became black like sackcloth of goat hair, and the whole moon turned blood red

Joel prophesies the sun turned to darkness and the moon to blood before the great and terrible day of the LORD (Joel 2:31), and Peter applies it at Pentecost (Acts 2:20). Darkened heavenly lights accompany the fall of Babylon (Isaiah 13:10), Egypt (Ezekiel 32:7-8) and Edom (Isaiah 34:4). God clothes the heavens with sackcloth (Isaiah 50:3). Assumption of Moses 10:5 has the sun darkened and the moon turned to blood at God's coming.
Eclipses were read as omens of the death of rulers and political upheaval in Greco-Roman culture. Sackcloth of black goat hair was the garment of mourning.

In the prophets, cosmic darkening accompanies the fall of nations under divine judgment (Isaiah 13; Ezekiel 32) and also the final day of the LORD (Joel 2-3). Whether the language here is symbolic of political collapse, describes literal cosmic disturbances, or both, is a central interpretive question.

Gentry, Chilton and others argue that because the prophets used this language for the historical fall of Babylon, Egypt and Edom, it here depicts the collapse of the Jewish commonwealth and temple order in AD 70, matching Matthew 24:29, 34.
Full preterists (following Russell) agree it portrays AD 70 and go further, identifying the sixth seal's 'great day' with the Parousia itself, fulfilled in that generation.
Futurists take the signs as literal or near-literal cosmic disturbances in the future tribulation that precede Christ's visible return (Matthew 24:29-30).
Elliott and Barnes read the sun, moon and stars as the ruling powers of pagan Rome, and their fall as the overthrow of paganism and its institutions under Constantine (AD 312-324).
Idealists and many eclectic interpreters (Beale) see a depiction of the final judgment at the end of history, though using imagery that could also describe intermediate judgments on nations.
The stars fell to the earth like unripe figs from a tree shaken by a great wind

Isaiah 34:4 pictures the host of heaven falling 'like fruit falling from a fig tree' when the LORD judges Edom and the nations. Stars often represent angelic or political powers (Daniel 8:10; Isaiah 14:12-13; 1 Enoch 86-88). The fig tree is also a common image for Israel (Jeremiah 24; Hosea 9:10; Mark 11:12-21).
Olynthoi were winter or late figs that often failed to ripen and dropped in spring storms.
The vivid simile shows the effortless ease with which God topples the heavenly and earthly powers. Preterists note the fig-tree link to Israel; others see only a nature image from Isaiah.
The sky receded like a scroll being rolled up; every mountain and island was moved

'The skies will roll up like a scroll' (Isaiah 34:4); mountains quake and melt before the LORD (Nahum 1:5; Jeremiah 4:23-26; Ezekiel 38:20). Psalm 102:25-26 speaks of heaven and earth wearing out like a garment and being changed. 1 Enoch 1:6 has high mountains shaken and made low at God's coming.
Ancient readers rolled scrolls on rods; a sky 'rolled up' is a striking image of the end of the visible order.

This is de-creation language, the old order dismantled before the Judge. Whether it describes the end of the world, the end of an age or regime, or both in typological sequence is the key question (see the chapter readings). The removal of mountains and islands recurs at the final bowl (16:20) and the last judgment (20:11).
The kings of the earth, the nobles, commanders, rich, mighty, every slave and free hid in the caves

Isaiah foretells people fleeing into caves of the rocks from the terror of the LORD when he rises to shake the earth, abandoning their idols (Isaiah 2:10, 19-21). Rulers of the earth face judgment in Isaiah 24:21 and Psalm 2:2. 1 Enoch 62:3-10 has the kings and mighty terrified before the Son of Man.
The sevenfold social list runs from client kings and Roman officials (megistanes, military tribunes/chiliarchs) down to slaves, spanning the whole hierarchy of Roman society.
Judgment reaches every rank, and the powerful who persecuted the saints are humbled. The seven categories signal completeness.
'Fall on us and hide us from the face of the One seated on the throne'

Hosea 10:8 has idolatrous Israel cry to the mountains 'Cover us' and to the hills 'Fall on us' at the destruction of Samaria's high places. Jesus quoted these words on the way to the cross, warning the daughters of Jerusalem of the coming calamity on their city (Luke 23:28-30).

Terror before God's face (presence) leads people to prefer being crushed than to face him. The quotation's history is important to interpreters, since its original and Gospel uses both concern the judgment of Israel.
Preterists stress that Jesus applied Hosea 10:8 specifically to Jerusalem's fall (Luke 23:28-30), making the sixth seal a picture of AD 70.
Futurists read it as the response of unbelievers worldwide at the future revelation of Christ's wrath, noting the universal scope ('kings of the earth').
Idealists and Beale see the final judgment on all who oppose God, with Hosea and Luke supplying the pattern of earlier historical judgments that foreshadow it.
The wrath of the Lamb; the great day of their wrath has come, and who is able to withstand it?

'The great day of the LORD' is a day of wrath (Zephaniah 1:14-18; Joel 2:11, 31). 'Who can endure it?' echoes Joel 2:11, Nahum 1:6 and Malachi 3:2. Psalm 2:12 warns rulers to honour the Son lest his wrath flare up.

The oxymoron 'wrath of the Lamb' shows that the sacrificial Lamb is also judge. The question 'who can stand?' is answered in chapter 7: those sealed by God and washed by the Lamb stand before the throne (7:9). Whether the 'great day' here is the final day or a historical day of the Lord is disputed.
A historical 'day of the Lord' on Jerusalem in AD 70, as Old Testament 'days of the LORD' fell on Babylon, Egypt and Edom.

The day of the Lord and the Parousia were fulfilled together in AD 70; there is no further end-of-history day, a view critics consider outside creedal orthodoxy because it denies a future bodily return, and which proponents defend from the New Testament time texts (Revelation 1:1, 3; 22:10).

Dispensationalists debate whether the wrath begins here or with the first seal; pretribulationists argue that the whole seventieth week is 'wrath', from which the church is exempt (1 Thessalonians 5:9), while prewrath writers (Rosenthal, Kurschner) place the start of God's wrath at the sixth seal.
Historicists see the day of wrath on pagan Rome's persecuting powers at the Constantinian revolution, a foreshadowing of the final day.
Idealists and Beale read the sixth seal as the last judgment itself, concluding the first cycle of judgments that the trumpets and bowls recapitulate.

Partial preterists (Gentry, Chilton, Gregg's preterist column) read the seals as Christ's covenant judgments on first-century Israel, closely matching the Olivet Discourse: false messiahs and conquest, war, famine and pestilence, the martyrdom of Christ's witnesses, and finally the collapse of the Jewish order in AD 70, described in prophetic de-creation language. 'Those who dwell upon the earth' are 'the inhabitants of the land'. Unlike full preterists, they hold that the final bodily return and last judgment are still future.

Full preterists (Russell, Preston) agree with the AD 70 setting but identify the sixth seal's 'great day of wrath' with the Second Coming itself, fulfilled in that generation (Matthew 16:27-28; 24:34). Critics note that this denies a future bodily return and resurrection affirmed in the historic creeds; proponents reply that the time texts require it and that the creeds must yield to Scripture.

Classic historicists (Elliott, Barnes) see six consecutive eras of Roman imperial history: prosperity under Nerva and the Antonines (white), civil war and military anarchy (red), crushing taxation (black), the death, plague and famine of AD 248-268 (pale), the Diocletianic persecution (fifth seal), and the overthrow of paganism under Constantine (sixth seal).

Dispensational futurists (Walvoord, Thomas) place the seals in the first half of the future seven-year tribulation: the Antichrist's rise, global war, famine and death, tribulation martyrs, and cosmic signs. Most pretribulationists see the seals as divine wrath from which the raptured church is exempt; prewrath futurists see the church present through the first five seals, with wrath beginning at the sixth seal. Historic premillennialists (Ladd) see the seals as characteristic of the age, intensifying before the end.
